content.thinking:
I need to write the whole file carefully in one pass since I can't test it, so I'm planning out a pixel-art monster truck design with realistic proportions scaled down—tire radius around 0.85, width 0.9, and matching overall height, length, and width ratios based on real monster truck dimensions.

I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy: a root chassis joint, front/rear axle joints, steering joints for the front wheels, and wheel joints as children, plus doors, hood, tailgate, and a simple pixel driver silhouette inside the cab. Working out how joint directions default when no explicit orientation is given, since that affects how bones inherit rotation from their parents.

For wheel geometry, I'm orienting the cylinder so its axis runs along X instead of the default Y, using a direction vector for the bone aim, and keeping the segment count low for a chunky pixel-art look. I'm also figuring out how the tread texture maps onto the cylinder's side UVs, accounting for the tire's circumference versus its width so the pixel texture doesn't stretch too badly.

Rather than relying on a stretched texture, I'm considering using cell-based painting for the tread blocks, computing angular segments from the UV coordinate to alternate colors around the tire and get a believable tread pattern without distortion.

Writing tyre paint logic...

I'm thinking body panels could use cellPaint for flames and gradients since the paint grid stays model-aligned on box geometry, so I'll set TEXEL to 0.05 for crisp body cells and 0.025 for finer details, keeping the pixel grid consistent across all parts while being mindful that texture-based decals also consume atlas space.

For door graphics, I'll avoid logos and instead paint a number like "13" using a small 3x5 pixel font, which is simpler than full text rendering. For the flame decals, I'm working out a function based on position along the side panel — flame height varies with a sawtooth tongue pattern rising from the front, so each cell's color depends on its z and y coordinates relative to the door bottom.

Now I'm working through the overall geometry layout in model space with the floor at y=0, figuring out wheel radius and center height so the wheels touch the floor properly given the cylinder's radial segmentation — making sure any sinking is negligible relative to the truck's scale.

Settling on 16 segments for a chunkier pixel-truck wheel, since both vertex-down and flat-bottom orientations keep sinking within tolerance. I also want to add blocky tread lugs around the tyre for extra detail rather than leaving it painted-tread only.

Still writing lug geometry...

I'll simplify by rotating the cylinder 90° about Z instead of using a direction vector, since Y maps to -X that way. For lug placement, I'm working out the radius (box outer edge at R+0.03) and figuring out how 16 lugs spaced at 22.5° intervals align so one sits at the bottom.

I'll set the tyre cylinder radius to 0.82 with lug boxes centered at radius 0.83, giving an outer lug radius of 0.88 and overall tyre diameter around 1.76 — close enough to a real monster truck tyre. I'm sinking the center height slightly (cy=0.875) so the lugs just touch the floor.

Now I'm working out lug placement: 16 positions spaced 22.5° apart around the tyre, with each lug's center computed from its angle and rotated about the X axis so the box orientation follows the tyre surface. I'm staggering the lugs side-to-side (x=±0.2) between alternating angles to mimic a tread pattern, checking that the widths don't leave too large a gap down the middle of the tyre.

I'm then offsetting the second row by half a step (11.25°) so the 32 total lugs interlock, verifying the tangential spacing at that radius leaves reasonable gaps between lugs, and confirming the lowest contact points still touch the ground properly at both row angles. Finally I'm deciding on coloring: a darker rubber tone for the tread lugs versus the main tyre body, plus defining sidewall cap regions based on distance from the axis for the painted rings.

Now I'm layering on the wheel rim itself—a chrome/yellow disc cylinder protruding slightly past the sidewall, with a dark inner hub ring, lug nut spheres, and a center cap, mirrored for left vs right wheel sides. I'm also sketching sidewall decoration ideas, like dashed whitewall stripe rings based on radial distance bands.

For the tread paint, I need to figure out which axis the normal points along so I can tell sidewall faces from tread faces, then use the cell's position to compute an angle index for banding. I'm adding worn rubber shading with noise, plus brownish mud splats concentrated near the bottom of the tire for extra realism.

Now I'm laying out the chassis frame: rail beams at x=±0.55, wheel hubs at y=0.875 with tops at 1.75, axle tubes connecting the wheels, and steering joints positioned at each wheel centre so the front wheels can pivot.

For wheel geometry, I'm placing the wheelbase at z=±1.75 and wheel centres at x=±1.45, with axle tubes running to about ±1.05 and spindles extending into the tyres, plus small steering knuckle boxes at the axle ends. Then I'm planning the coilover shocks angling from the axle points up and inward to the chassis, with a yellow rod body and chrome shaft to get that classic monster truck look.

For the coil spring look, I'm thinking of stacking thin disc cylinders along the shock axis rather than trying a true spiral sweep, using transform matrices to position each disc and merging them into one geometry per shock. I'm also deciding to just attach the shocks statically to the chassis bone rather than worry about rigging them to move with the axle, since that's not critical for the look.

Now I'm working out the suspension linkage: keeping the axles as hinge joints, adding trailing-arm rods between axle and chassis for the four-link setup, and sketching the chassis frame rail heights and positions relative to the axle and body mounts.

I'm figuring out the body dimensions so the pickup cab and bed fit narrower than the tire track, checking clearances against the front and rear tire positions so the body doesn't clip the wheels.

I'm blocking out the body geometry into a lower tub, a raised cab section, and a hood, stacking their height ranges so the pickup shell reads with distinct panel lines along the z-axis.

For the hood I'm making it a separate hinged part—a thin plate near the top of the engine bay that pivots at the cowl line along the x-axis, relying on default joint orientation for the hinge rotation. Below it I'm adding a front grille block and skipping fender flares since the tires sit outside the body mesh, then moving on to define the cab's z-range.

For the cab I'm thinking through overall height: tire tops at 1.75, roof around 2.8, plus a light bar pushing total height to roughly 2.95, which is close to real monster truck proportions. For the windshield I'm planning to extrude the cab's side silhouette (z-y profile) across the x-width, so the slanted glass comes out as a stepped pixel-style staircase, and figuring out how painting on those extruded faces would need to map model coordinates to the correct face.

I'm considering extruding the whole pickup body (hood, cab, bed) as one side profile piece and using paint to add windows, doors, flames, and bed rails directly onto it, then adding separate thin door panels slightly proud of the body that hinge about a vertical axis at the A-pillar, matching the body's paint so the doors blend seamlessly.

I'm sizing the door panel and painting a glass window region with a diagonal reflection highlight, but weighing whether to bother with a visible interior or just keep the glass opaque for simplicity since full interior detail seems too complex for this scale.

I'll keep it simple: just one driver visible on the +X door with a steering wheel, skip adding a passenger. Now I should pin down the actual coordinates for the design more precisely.

Working out the body profile, I define a grid unit of 0.05 so dimensions snap to that size, then set up the extrusion direction and cross-product math to get the side profile oriented correctly and centered symmetrically before laying out the actual outline points.

Still writing profile columns...

I'll exclude the bed from the main extruded profile, limiting it to cab and hood, and build the bed separately from floor, sidewall, tailgate, and front wall boxes — adding details like a toolbox, spare tyre, and roll bar light.

Now I'm defining the height profile along the z-axis for the cab roof, windshield slope, cowl, hood, and nose/grill sections, mapping out the top surface heights segment by segment.

I'm also considering making the hood a separate lid sitting slightly above the body profile, which would open up the idea of a visible engine bay underneath—maybe with a supercharger blower poking through a hood scoop for a classic muscle car look.

For the windshield I'm figuring out a stepped approximation to the slope since the geometry is extruded in columns, and for the cab sides I'm deciding whether windows and door outlines get painted directly onto the body surface rather than modeled as separate door panels.

I'll make the doors a slightly raised overlay (proud of the body by about 0.025-0.05 in x) carrying the full door paint—glass, handle, number, flames—while keeping the same `bodyPaint` function underneath for consistency, so the seam between door and body stays invisible when they align.

Now I'm working out the glass regions by position: side windows get defined by z and y ranges that follow the sloped roofline, with the glass top edge tracking the roof curve minus a small margin, and the door cutout spanning roughly z -0.1 to 0.85.

Then I'm figuring out the windshield glass painting, which involves checking stair-step risers between z 0.35 and 0.95 for the sloped front.

I'll add a diagonal streak pattern for lighter glass highlights, plus a rear cab window using the back-face normal. Now I need to settle on the final architecture and color palette before writing the full code carefully, given how long this file is getting.

For colors, I'm keeping flat color count under 64 and choosing a bold scheme: electric blue body (#2b63e8) with darker and lighter blue shades, orange-yellow flame accents (#ff7a1a, #ffd23a), red highlights, white, and black for the frame.

Rounding out the palette with grays and chrome for metal parts, dark rubber for tires, brown mud tones, and yellow rims to complement the blue body — plus glowing white/yellow for headlights, light bars, and tail lights. I'm also estimating the total painted surface area (body, bed, hood, tires) at roughly 60 m² to figure out the right texel density for a 2048² texture, landing on a cell size around 0.025-0.05m for good resolution.

Now I'm setting up imports for the build script — Three.js core, geometry merging utilities, the builder function, the glow kit, and various pixel-art painting helpers like bayer dithering, cell painting, and pixel text tools, making sure I only pull in what's actually used to avoid unused-import errors.

Then I'm defining metadata for the model (name, description, style, commit hash) and texel size constants for fine detail, followed by a color palette for the monster truck — blues for the body, oranges and yellows for flame effects, laid out as hex constants.

I'm continuing the palette with yellow, steel, iron, rubber, and glass color ramps, then sketching a body paint function that assigns colors based on region, starting with a profile function that steps the cab height based on z-position.

Defining the cab roofline...

I'm adding a lid above the hood bay, 0.1 thick, extending from z=0.95 to 2.4, and setting up the extrude call that builds the cab body along the proper axis orientation with the correct thickness and bone attachment.

I'm checking dimensions — cab width stays at 1.9 across x=±0.95, matching the bed walls and doors, with the cab-plus-hood length totaling 2.4. Now I'm working out the paint function for the body, evaluating color based on the cell's center position, axis, and normal to distinguish the side faces.

Writing shading logic...

Still shaping the flame geometry...

Working out thresholds so yellow sits deepest near the base, orange in the middle band, and red along the edges, with flames anchored where the body meets the fire. I'm also considering adding a thin dark sill line beneath the flame base for contrast.

I need to constrain the flames so they only paint onto the lower body panels, below the window line, and not spill onto the cab roof or hood. The hood itself gets a separate racing-stripe treatment with a central orange stripe and white accent lines rather than flame coloring.

I'm extending the stripe logic up across the roof and bed top so it reads as one continuous racing stripe, plus adding darker pinstripe outlines along the bottom edge. I'm also considering whether to paint a number or roundel on the doors using a tiny pixel-font sampled against the z/y coordinates, positioned above the flame zone and below the window.

Still designing glyphs... now I need to work out the orientation of the digits so they read correctly from the viewer's perspective looking at the +X face.

I'm now working out the roundel's grid dimensions in texel units, figuring out the z-range for the plate and how wide the glyph block should be within it, with margins on each side.

I'm laying out the digit columns with gaps between pairs to fit within the 10-cell width, and matching rows to a 9-cell height with symmetric margins. I'll draw the plate with a black border ring, white interior, and dark blue digits, then work out where the vertical placement intersects the glass's lower edge.

Now I'm figuring out the door shape, since it needs to follow the sloped roofline profile rather than being a plain rectangle—extruding a stepped outline from the cab profile so the top edge matches the roof curve while the bottom sits at a fixed height.

Writing extrusion coordinates...

I'm placing the hinge joint on the door's front edge near the top, aligning it with the body frame, and planning a small handle box protruding near the front face at a mid-height position.

I need to resolve the z-range conflicts between the handle, roundel, and window panels on the door, adjusting the roundel to span z∈[0.25,0.75] and the handle to sit at z∈[0.06,0.2] so they don't overlap, and extending the side window glass further along the door's height and depth.

Now I'm sketching the full chassis part list: frame rails as paired boxes running the length of the body in iron tones, cross members spaced along z, and gusset details, planning to build these out as individual box geometries positioned relative to a chassis root bone.

I'm figuring out the mounting gap between the chassis and body, adding mount posts, then moving on to axle components -- housing tubes, differential pumpkins as spheres with cover boxes, driveshafts as thin rods connecting the chassis center to front and rear axles, plus a transfer case box.

For the engine, I'm placing a block box under the hood within the engine bay, then adding a blower poking through the hood with a scoop opening, and considering chrome exhaust stacks rising from the hood sides with flared cone tops.

Realizing the solid body extrude fills the entire engine bay region, which would bury any engine geometry inside it. Rather than modeling a separate engine, I'll just paint the top surface of that bay area with a dark engine-colored texture suggesting pipework, so lifting the hood reveals something convincing without wasted geometry.

I'll construct the hood lid as four separate box segments (front, back, left, right) that leave a rectangular hole in the middle, through which a blower mounted on the chassis pokes up. Working out the dimensions and positions for each of the four lid pieces around that hole now...

Now I'm sketching the blower assembly itself: a steel base box, a chrome scoop on top, a dark intake opening, plus pulley and velocity-stack details, while keeping the hinge joint at the hood's back edge so it can still swing open normally.

For the exhaust stacks, I'm placing two per side poking up through slots in the hood lid (since the hood itself is static relative to the chassis, this works fine), using tapered rods with flared chrome tops and dark open discs to suggest hollow pipe ends.

For the cab and bed, I'm skipping interior detail since the driver covers that, and focusing on the truck bed structure: a floor box sitting just above the body bottom, side walls rising from it, and a front wall placed right behind the cab to define where the bed interior begins.

Now I'm adding a roll bar and light bar on the roof for a rugged look, then working out the tailgate as a hinged panel at the bed's rear, positioning its joint and panel dimensions to match the bed opening.

I'm also laying out the bed walls and floor dimensions, adding chrome rail caps on top of the side walls, and brainstorming bed contents like a toolbox or cargo crates to fill the space.

Then I'm placing a rear bumper box and a heavy front bull bar with a pushbar cage, roughing out positions and sizes to match the body's front and rear z-extents, and considering adding a winch up front.

Now I'm detailing the grille pattern with alternating dark horizontal slats framed in blue, and positioning glowing headlight boxes near the front face with chrome bezels underneath for contrast.

I'm checking how the body front face aligns with the headlight and grille placement vertically, making sure the tires sit just outside the narrower body width so wheel arches aren't needed structurally.

I'm reconsidering the body half-width — tightening it to 0.9 so there's a small visible gap between the body and the tire's inner face, keeping the axle area slightly exposed near the frame rails, and double-checking that the front tire's z-range sits properly beside the hood/nose section without major overlap issues.

Setting wheel centers at z=±1.7 keeps the wheelbase around 3.4m, which lines up with real truck proportions, with the rear tire sitting beside the bed and the front tire extending just past the body front, matching where a bumper would be. I'm placing the axle at the wheel center position and starting to work out the steering tie-rod geometry connecting to the front axle.

Now I'm thinking through shock absorber placement, two per axle, and realizing the body geometry creates a conflict: shocks need to connect from the axle up toward the frame, but the body's solid lower section would intrude on that path if mounted too far inward. I'm considering moving the shock mounts further outward, sandwiched between the body side and tire, to avoid the collision with the body panel.

Actually I should raise the body higher above the tyres to get that classic monster truck proportion, with lots of visible chassis and suspension showing underneath—that's the iconic look I want.

Setting body bottom at 1.95, cab roof at 3.2, hood top around 2.6, and light bar hitting 3.4, giving a realistic overall height near 3.4m and a truck length of 5.2m. I'm placing the frame rails, mounting posts, and shocks with specific coordinates so the suspension geometry reads correctly from the side view.

Now I'm working out the shock tower geometry — adding a vertical plate and bracket box near the rail, then defining the lower and upper shock mount points with a slight inward lean so the shock connects properly to the axle bracket. I'm laying out the shock's cylinder segments along the mount-to-mount vector to represent the body and shaft.

I'm building the coil spring as a stack of flat discs along the shock axis, sized to feel chunky for the pixel-art style, with cap discs at each end for the spring seats, and sketching out a helper to orient each disc along the shock's direction without relying on the discouraged quaternion method.

Placing merged geometries with a `merge(list)` helper wrapping `mergeGeometries` and guarding against null results, since cylinders, boxes, and spheres all produce mergeable indexed geometry once transformed.

I'm considering whether to flatten shading via `flat: true`, converting indexed geometry to non-indexed and recomputing vertex normals for crisp cylindrical facets, while checking that painted-color parts still work correctly alongside flat shading and merged geometry.

I'm designing a small bucketing helper that groups geometry by bone and color into buckets, then flushes each bucket into a merged part with the right flat/bone/name settings, while deciding which parts (like glowing or textured ones) need to bypass the bucket system and be added directly.

I'm also sketching out a tiny pixel font for a license plate texture, mapping glyphs for digits and a handful of letters so I can render simple plate text like "M0N5T3R" onto the truck.

Then I'm placing a rear plate as a textured plane mounted on the tailgate's back face, positioned and oriented to sit flush against it.

Now I'm setting up a body-bottom reference height (BY = 1.95) and deriving the other key vertical positions from it -- roof, hood bay, lid, and cowl tops -- so I can keep all the dimensions consistent as I build out the rest.

I'm defining a cabTop function that interpolates between the roof height, the cowl, and the windshield slope depending on z-position, then using it to compute the profile cell heights column by column across the body from the rear to the front, converting each height difference into discrete 0.05-unit cells.

For the doors, I'm working out their position and thickness relative to the body sides, placing them at the correct height band between the floor and cab roofline, with the front edge aligned to where the windshield slope meets the cowl. I'm also setting up the shared paint function to carve out door window glass within a bounded z and y range.

Now I'm shifting to the truck bed: sizing the floor box, side walls, and tailgate within a z-range behind the cab, positioning the tailgate hinge joint at the bottom rear of the bed.

Working out the frame rails and mounting posts beneath the bed, then placing the rear cab window and roll bar hoop behind it, checking their positions relative to the bed front wall.

For the bed body, I'm planning the flame decal envelope to sweep from the nose back toward the cab but stop before the bed region so the painted panels there stay clean with rivet lines instead.

Now I'm figuring out how to distinguish inner vs outer bed wall faces using the normal direction and sign of x, applying a darker ribbed steel paint to the interior and the body color outside, then working out how to stamp panel gap lines (like door seams) onto specific z-cell positions using cell index math.

Defining color palettes and the body paint function...

I'll use dithering on strong gradients to get checker-style pixel transitions, then start defining cases in order, beginning with glass areas like side windows based on axis and position checks.

For the actual window regions, I'm setting bounds on the door and body side faces, plus the rear quarter window, then computing the glass color using a diagonal gradient with streak bands mapped to different palette indices.

Still writing driver figure logic...

Working out the window and glass boundaries on the door, checking the vertical extent against roofline and matching the driver's head position within that frame.

Still defining windshield and cell logic...

Now I'm working out the front grille and headlight region, checking face normals and coordinate ranges to alternate slat colors for a grille pattern.

Assigning bezel and valance colors...

Mapping out top-face regions for the hood, roof, and open engine bay, with stripe colors determined by position along the hood and a gradient pipe pattern for the engine bay interior.

Adding hood louvers and door panel gap lines...

I need to raise the window sill to fit the roundel properly, giving the door lower region about 0.45 units. I'm working out the roundel's grid dimensions, aiming for roughly 8 cells tall with margins for the border.

Actually, this feels too cramped on the door. Let me try putting the number roundels on the bed side walls instead, which have about 0.5 units of vertical space—9 rows would fit nicely with proper padding. I'll keep the door simpler with just flames and a chrome handle, put number roundels on both bed sides, and extend flames across the body from front to the door area.

For the flames, I'm defining an envelope function that tapers based on z-position, strongest near the hood and fading toward the rear, with a tongue/tooth pattern creating the licking flame shape using phase and fractional calculations.

Still refining color ramp logic...

Doors use the same coloring function, with the driver-side condition only applying on the +X side using a sign check. For the bed, I'm defining outward-facing wall detection and wall thickness near x=±0.85...

Now I'm working out the roundel number plate's position on the bed's side wall, figuring out the z-range and y-range in cell units so I can map local plate coordinates for rendering the number pattern.

Working out the index mapping...

For rows I'm computing which row from the top corresponds to a given y coordinate. Then I'm laying out the glyph grid: border cells (edge rows/columns) get the black/iron material, interior cells are white, and I'm figuring out which columns hold the digit strokes given the 10-wide grid with margins and gaps between digits.

Actually, switching to an 11-wide, 9-row grid so two digits fit cleanly with margins, gaps, and border cells on all sides. I'm mapping the digit font rows into this grid, deciding the digit color against the white interior, and treating corner cells as the base body color to round them off visually. For the inner faces, I'm picking a dark iron color ramp with slight noise variation and adding periodic rib lines along the surface.

Now I'm figuring out the truck bed exterior — a blue gradient base with rivet columns, a highlighted rail along the top edge, and vertical stamping lines spaced every so many cells. For the tailgate I'm deciding on a painted panel matching the bed color with an embossed horizontal band, plus reflector details, while the bed floor gets a ribbed steel pattern using the iron ramp with ribs spaced every four cells.

Writing tire paint function...

For the sidewall I'm mapping out concentric radius bands moving outward from the bead to the shoulder, mixing in lettering marks that only appear on alternating angular segments, some mud spatter, and a darker shoulder ring near the tread edge. For the tread itself I'm setting up a lug pattern repeating every 22.5 degrees with extra lug box geometry layered on top of the base rubber color.

Now I'm figuring out the mud coloring based on noise and vertical position so the tire looks muddier toward the bottom, using a ramp of brown tones, and defining a separate darker ramp for the plain rubber. I'm starting to lay out the wheel's physical components, beginning with the tire cylinder geometry and its rotation and placement on the wheel joint.

Adding lugs and rim geometry...

Still working out the wheel rim layering...

Adding wheel spokes as thin rods from hub to rim, and noting only the outer face needs the recess detail since the inner face stays hidden.

Defining the wheel and chassis joints...

Defining the wheel joint position, then moving to doors and hood hinges—door hinges rotate about Y at the chassis sides, and the hood hinge sits centered near the front.

I'm settling on roughly 14 joints covering the chassis, axles, steering, wheels, doors, hood, and tailgate, with side naming based on positive/negative x. Now I'm sketching the roof light bar geometry, positioning a small box near the top of the roof.

Adding lamp pod details...

Thinking about a roof antenna with a small pennant flag, but capping its height around 3.5-3.6 to keep proportions sane for the rig.

Now I'm adding side mirrors attached to each door with a rod arm and a flat mirror box, plus chrome door handles positioned on the lower door panel, skipping wheel wells for now.

Moving underneath, I'm laying out the chassis frame rails running the length of the body, cross members connecting them at several z-positions using iron rods, and starting on the body mount posts.

Still placing underbelly components...

Still placing axle components...

Now I'm adding mud buildup using noise-based splatter near the lower body, applying it where height and noise thresholds suggest grime accumulation along sills, doors, bed underside, tires, and axles.

Then I'm designing the front bumper with an iron box frame, chrome bull-bar hoop rods, tow hooks, and a winch assembly with drum and fairlead, plus a simpler rear bumper box with a tow shackle and glowing red tail lights.

For the taillights, I'm positioning glowing red boxes on the tailgate edges bolted to the chassis, skipping fuel details, and keeping wheel nuts simple. For the suspension, I'm giving the shock bodies a yellow finish with orange-red spring coils and a small nitrogen reservoir attached to the chassis bones.

I'm also sketching out the shock tower plates and mounting points so they align with the frame rails without clipping, plus adding a toolbox and bed liner texture inside the truck bed for interior detail.

For decals, I'm considering a generic pixel skull-and-crossbones sticker for the tailgate alongside a license plate, positioning both within the tailgate's visible area so they don't overlap.

Designing the skull pixel art...

Still designing the pixel grid pattern, verifying each row is 11 characters wide...

Finishing the row verification, all checks out, including the teeth row. Now I'm planning the license plate texture: a 22x11 pixel grid with a dark border and light yellow background, with "MUD13" rendered using 3x5 pixel glyphs spaced to fit the width.

Writing glyph definitions...

Still placing the plate texture...

I'm placing the skull decal plane at a small size near the rear, and considering whether to skip extra stickers like a hood sticker or number roundel for simplicity, maybe adding a "13" roundel on the roof instead.

I'm deciding to skip the light bar, wheelie bar tubes, parachute, and sun visor details for now, but I'll include sidewall tire text and add a thin antenna rod rising from the rear deck.

For the flag at the top, I'm sizing a small box geometry and applying a checkered texture so it reads as a tiny racing flag, relying on the box's face mapping to display the pattern cleanly on its front faces.

Now I'm settling the overall proportions: truck body around 3.4 units tall, antenna rising to 3.5, flag spanning roughly 3.5 to 3.66, and total height landing near 3.66. With the dimensions settled, I'm starting to write the actual TypeScript module, setting up imports for geometry merging, glow effects, pixel art utilities, and math helpers needed to build the scene.

I'm deciding to use the rng import for scattering small mud clod boxes around the lower tread area of each wheel, planning around 14 clumps per wheel positioned within a random angle range near the bottom of the tire.

Now I'm sketching out small geometry helper functions for boxes, cylinders, and spheres that build and position primitive shapes using transform matrices, to assemble the mud clumps and other parts efficiently.

I'm then designing a bucketing system that groups geometries by bone and color so they can be merged into single parts per material, flushing each bucket into a `b.part` call with the merged, flattened geometry. I'm weighing whether the tyre's cylinder geometry should stay smooth-shaded rather than flattened, since low-poly pixel style might look better with faceted normals there.

I also need to make sure color types across the paint helpers line up with whatever `Fill` type `b.part` expects, likely narrowing down to `string | Paint` rather than the broader `ColorInput` to avoid type errors, since cell paint functions already resolve to usable colors from fixed palettes.

Now I'm sketching cabin geometry constants (heights and taper curve) and a glass-tint function that cycles through a gradient palette based on cell position, plus a mud-overlay helper that blends noise with a vertical falloff to decide when grime appears.

Writing bodyColor function...

Still refining window boundaries...

Still refining the color logic... now adding windshield glass detection based on surface normal and position.

Adding front grille pattern...

Still defining bezel colors...

The engine bay stays hidden unless the hood is open, revealing it through the hole beneath the blower. The hood lid and roof get their own top-surface stripe treatment based on height and normal, with a generic fallback top color picked using the surface normal's y-component.

Defining the stripe thresholds based on axis position, mapping ranges to orange, dark blue pinstripe, and yellow bands. For the sides, I'm setting up gap lines between door panels using a grid of cells along the z-axis, applying edge markers at specific cell indices near the front and rear of the door.

Now I'm working on the window belt trim, figuring out which row of cells corresponds to the chrome sill versus the dark blue pinstripe beneath it, calculating cell centers from the relative y position to make sure the row boundaries line up cleanly.

Writing flame gradient logic...

I need to double check that the flame region doesn't overlap the door's chrome sill row near rel 0.475, since flames cap around 0.5.

Working out layer order: glass, lines, trim, then mud on top of flames at the bottom for a weathering effect, then the base.

I'm writing the base color function, picking from a blue palette weighted by surface normal, relative height, and noise for a dithered metallic look. Now I'm drafting the bed color function, checking outward-facing panels based on x-axis sign and normal direction.

For the bed itself, top-facing cells get a floor color below a certain height or a lighter rail color above it, while the underside gets a dark near-black shade. I'm adding ribbing detail to the floor using modular checks on the cell's u/v coordinates to create a repeating pattern.

For the side panels, I'm distinguishing inward and outward-facing surfaces, giving outward ones a roundel or blue paneling with mud accents near the bottom, and inward ones a ribbed deck color gradient. For the rear/tailgate, I'm adding horizontal embossed rows with chrome edging and a blue base tone.

Still working through the z-axis logic, separating tailgate styling from front wall and bed interior faces, then placing a roundel decal on the outward side within a defined z/y window using index rounding to position it.

Mapping the roundel grid into border pixels, interior fill, and a two-digit glyph pattern drawn from a font lookup, with border cells getting a dark outline and interior pixels defaulting to cream unless a glyph pixel is set to the dark blue color.

Now I'm checking material assignments for body parts—hood, bed, cab, doors all pulling from the body/bed color variables correctly—and working out the cab's extrusion spans by computing height differences across columns, rounding to grid units, and validating overlap conditions between neighboring spans before placing the hood lid geometry.

Also painting the underside facing down as iron. Then I'm adding the hood as a separate box part attached to its own bone, centered with its own UV mapping, before moving on to the engine and blower parts on the chassis bone.

Now I'm setting up the glowing headlight lenses as small boxes on the chassis, positioning them so their front face aligns with the cab profile at z=2.4.
